text: Neural ODEs replace discrete hidden-state updates with neural-network dynamics integrated by a numerical solver. Adjoint training reconstructs states alongside gradients in a reverse-time augmented ODE, avoiding storage of intermediate solver operations and making memory independent of the number of function evaluations. Solver tolerances trade precision for computation. On MNIST, 0.42% test error with 0.22 million parameters, versus a residual network's 0.41% with 0.60 million, supports comparable classification with fewer parameters rather than improved accuracy. For dynamics uniformly Lipschitz in state and continuous in time, the instantaneous change-of-variables theorem expresses log-density evolution through a Jacobian trace rather than a determinant. Trace additivity permits continuous normalizing flows with density-update cost linear in hidden units per function evaluation; two-dimensional experiments illustrate density fitting and reversible sampling. A latent ODE uses shared continuous dynamics to evaluate irregularly observed trajectories at arbitrary times and can jointly model observation times through a Poisson likelihood. On synthetic noisy spirals with 30 of 100 observations, RMSE is 0.1642 versus 0.3937 for an RNN across 100 prediction times extending beyond training observations, supporting sparse-observation prediction in this setting. Reverse-time reconstruction can introduce numerical error; checkpointing mitigates it by storing intermediate states.

FlexGen targets bulk language-model generation when weights and key-value caches exceed GPU memory. Reusing each loaded layer across blocks of batches amortizes weight transfers; offloading caches as well as weights permits larger batches than weight-only offloading. A cost model and linear-programming search select placements across GPU, CPU, and disk and batch sizes. Without CPU computation and neglecting activation I/O, the implemented schedule has asymptotic weight I/O within twice optimal. On synthetic OPT-175B generation with 512-token prompts and 32-token outputs, a 16-GB T4 with 208-GB host memory and SSD achieves 0.69 generated tokens/s, versus 0.01 for unquantized Accelerate and DeepSpeed, supporting throughput-oriented offloading beyond model fitting. Group-wise 4-bit weight/cache compression avoids disk swapping and raises throughput to 1.12 tokens/s without retraining or calibration. These benchmarks use dummy weights; separate real-weight Lambada and WikiText tests show small quality changes with 4-bit compression and sparse value-cache loading, whereas 3-bit compression does not preserve accuracy. Compression is not uniformly faster. Four-GPU pipelining yields superlinear decoding scaling but sublinear total-generation scaling for OPT-30B and OPT-175B with 32-token outputs. The gains depend on host memory and favor bulk throughput over low-latency generation.

FlexGen targets batch inference when large language model weights and key-value caches exceed GPU memory. Offloading caches permits larger batches, while processing multiple GPU batches with each loaded layer amortizes weight transfers. A cost model and linear programming select tensor placement across GPU, CPU, and disk. Without CPU computation, an idealized analysis bounds asymptotic weight I/O within twice the optimum. In dummy-weight OPT-175B benchmarks with 512-token prompts and 32 generated tokens, FlexGen achieves 0.69 tokens/s uncompressed, versus 0.01 for uncompressed Accelerate and DeepSpeed, on one 16-GB T4 with 208-GB CPU memory and a 1.5-TB SSD. Four-bit weight and cache compression without retraining or calibration raises throughput to 1.12 tokens/s by fitting tensors in host memory and avoiding disk transfers. Separate real-weight Lambada and WikiText evaluations show small quality changes, including with sparse value-cache access, but compression can slow models fitting GPU memory. Four-GPU offloading yields super-linear decoding scaling but sublinear overall scaling for 32-token generation. Completing seven HELM sub-scenarios with OPT-IML-30B in 21 hours, including overhead, establishes an end-to-end batch use case beyond synthetic throughput tests. The throughput gains suit workloads accepting long completion times and depend on host-memory capacity and storage bandwidth.

Neural ordinary differential equations parameterize hidden-state evolution continuously and obtain outputs with a black-box ODE solver. Adjoint training solves an augmented ODE backward, reconstructing states instead of storing solver operations, so memory is independent of function-evaluation count. Solver tolerances trade numerical accuracy for computation. On MNIST, an ODE network reaches 0.42% test error with 0.22 million parameters, versus 0.41% with 0.60 million for a residual network: continuous-depth training retains comparable classification performance with fewer parameters. For dynamics uniformly Lipschitz in state and continuous in time, an instantaneous change-of-variables theorem makes log-density evolution depend on a Jacobian trace instead of a determinant. Because traces add across additive dynamics, continuous normalizing flows can widen with density-update cost linear in hidden-unit count; toy experiments illustrate reversible sampling and density estimation. A latent generative model uses shared dynamics to define trajectories at arbitrary observation times and incorporates Poisson likelihoods for observation timing. With 30 irregularly sampled observations from synthetic spirals, predictive RMSE is 0.1642 versus 0.3937 for an RNN, supporting extrapolation from irregular observations using continuous latent dynamics. Backward reconstruction can introduce numerical error; checkpointing trades storage for reconstruction accuracy.
